Learning Objectives
Describe the epidemiology, pathophysiology, and presentation of spinal metastatic disease.
Discuss scoring systems for spinal metastatic disease.
Review treatment algorithms for spinal metastases.
Overview and Epidemiology
Incidence
Bone is the third most common site of metastatic disease (after the lungs and liver).1
The spine is the most common location for of bony metastases (followed by the pelvis, ribs,
and extremities; Figure 1).
Demographics: bony metastatic lesions most common in patients older than 40 years.2

Overview and Epidemiology
Of the 1.2 million cancers newly diagnosed in the United States each year, 10% to 30%
are associated with symptomatic spinal metastases on presentation.3 In addition,
symptomatic spinal metastatic disease is the initial manifestation of malignancy in 12%
to 20% of patients, and the most common malignant lesions in the spine are metastases
from another site.4 After the lungs and liver, the skeletal system is the third most
common site for metastases; of those, the spine is the most common site of skeletal
metastatic disease. In autopsy studies, vertebral metastases have been present in more
than one-third of patients with cancer.5 The malignant lesions that are most likely to

metastasize to the spine, in descending order, are breast (spine metastases develop in
16% to 37% of patients with breast cancer), lung (12% to 15%), prostate (9% to 15%),
kidney (3% to 6%), and thyroid (4%).6 These lesions typically are symptomatic if they
involve the thoracic (68% to 70%), lumbosacral (16% to 22%), and cervical (8% to 15%)
spine.7
Pathophysiology
Batson Venous Plexus
Metastatic bone lesions can be osteolytic or osteoblastic.
Osteolytic bone lesions typically are caused by tumor-induced activation of osteoclasts,
which occurs via the receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Β, receptor activator of
nuclear factor kappa-Β ligand, and osteoprotegerin cascade.8
An oncogenic cell releases cytokines interleukin-6, interleukin-11, and parathyroid
hormone-related peptide in the presence of transforming growth factor beta.
Transforming growth factor beta–mediated release of parathyroid hormone-related
peptide and interleukin-11 activates osteoblasts.
Osteoblasts secrete receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Β ligand, which binds to
receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-Β on osteoclasts and activates osteoclasts.
Osteoblastic bone metastases usually are observed in patients with prostate or breast
cancer.9
Prostate cancer cells secrete endothelin 1.
Endothelin 1 binds to endothelin A receptor on osteoblasts and stimulates osteoblasts.
Endothelin 1 decreases WNT suppressor Dickkopf-related protein 1, which activates the
WNT pathway and, therefore, increases osteoblast activity.
Symptoms on Presentation
Pain: Most common manifestation 10
Two common types
Mechanical because of bone destruction
Tumorigenic caused by growth factors that are released by the tumor cells and create
inflammation

Patients often report axial night pain.
Metastatic hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia also may have some psychiatric manifestations, such as emotional instability,
confusion, delirium, psychosis, and stupor.
Symptoms are more common with higher calcium levels (12 mg/dL [3 mmol/L])..
Severe hypercalcemia (>15 to 16 mg/dL [3.75 to 4 mmol/L]) is considered a medical
emergency; affected patients may experience coma and/or cardiac arrest.

Symptoms on Presentation
The neuromuscular symptoms of hypercalcemia are caused by a negative resetting of
muscle membranes secondary to the increased interaction between calcium and sodium
channels. Calcium blocks sodium channels and inhibits depolarization of nerve and
muscle fibers; therefore, the increase in calcium raises the threshold for depolarization.
This results in diminished deep tendon reflexes (hyporeflexia) and skeletal muscle
weakness. Patients also may experience cardiac arrhythmias (especially if prescribed
digoxin), fatigue, nausea, emesis, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, and paralytic ileus.
This is called the bathmotropic effect.
Evaluation
The diagnostic workup for patients with spinal bony metastatic disease is similar to that for
patients with a single bone lesion of unknown primary origin (Figure 2).

Physical Examination
Neurologic deficits: Patients may present with various neurologic deficits, depending on the
level of involvement. A detailed neuromotor examination is recommended in patients with
spinal metastatic disease11 (Resource 1).
Focal tenderness: Patients may have focal tenderness at the location of the metastatic disease;
however, this is not always a presenting symptom.
Hyperreflexia (upper motor neuron) or hyporeflexia (because of hypercalcemia)

Radiography
AP and lateral radiographs of the spine in the region of pain in flexion and extension
Lytic or blastic morphology
Lung, thyroid, and renal lesions are primarily lytic.

Bone Scintigraphy
Whole-body imaging to allow for evaluation for other sites of metastatic bony involvement
Multiple myeloma, renal cell carcinoma, and thyroid carcinoma often appear cold on bone
scans because of their hypervascular nature and relative paucity of osteoblastic activity. A
skeletal survey is a better test for these histologies.
MRI With and Without Contrast of Contrast of the Spine
Contrast may help delineate tumor tissue from scar tissue at sites of previous spinal surgery
and help identify necrosis.

gadolinium dye or contraindications to MRI.
Positron Emission Tomography
This imaging modality is used for certain indications (such as lymphoma) as a baseline staging
scan. It is not the standard staging imaging modality at most institutions for most cancers,
other than lymphoma.
Laboratory Tests
Complete blood count with differential
Basic metabolic panel
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
Liver function tests, calcium level, phosphate level, and alkaline phosphatase level
Serum and urine immunoelectrophoresis
Biopsy

Laboratory Tests
In general, in all patients with bony metastatic disease, if the primary carcinoma is not
identified, a biopsy is necessary to rule out a primary bone lesion. This is critical because
management may be very different.
Anatomic Considerations
Thoracic Spine
Risk of fracture/collapse exists if 50% to 60% of the vertebral body is involved (without other
abnormalities).
Risk of fracture/collapse exists if 20% to 30% of the vertebral body is involved and the
costovertebral joint is involved.


Thoracic Spine
Symptomatic spine lesions are more common in the thoracic spine (68% to 70%) than
the lumbar spine (16% to 22%) and the cervical spine (15%).14 The risk of neurologic
compromise is the greatest in the thoracic spine because this area has the smallest
canal-to-cord size ratio. In addition, the blood supply to the spinal cord is the most
tenuous between the fourth and ninth thoracic vertebrae, making a vascular injury to
the cord more likely.15 Typically, 50% of the vertebral body must be involved to be
observed on radiographs; therefore, MRI or CT should be performed in patients with
intractable back pain and a known cancer diagnosis. This also is true for the cervical and
lumbar spine.14
Lumbar Spine
Risk of fracture/collapse exists if 35% to 40% of the vertebral body is involved (without other
abnormalities).
Risk of fracture/collapse exists if 25% of vertebral body is involved and the pedicle/posterior
element is involved.

Lumbar Spine
Although only 16% to 22% of metastatic spine lesions are in the lumbar spine,
biomechanical and anatomic features specific to the lumbar spine, such as the large size
and high weight-bearing demand of the lumbar vertebral bodies, must be considered
during surgical fixation. The lumbar nerve roots also innervate muscles that are essential
to ambulation and cannot be routinely sacrificed during surgery. In a retrospective study
of patients who underwent surgical treatment, specifically patients with metastases to
the lumbar spine, Tomita et al16 reported that 94% had a considerable reduction in pain
and 79% of the nonambulatory patients regained the ability to ambulate.

Classification Systems
Classification systems have become standardized in the field of spine oncology to guide
evidence-based treatment decisions.
Spine tumor classification systems have evolved to reflect improved understanding of tumor
biology and the evolving role of radiosurgery (focal, high-dose radiation therapy) as a
treatment option for select patients and tumors.
Several classification systems exist, each of which has varying focus:
Anatomic tumor characteristics: Harrington classification for spinal metastases15
Systemic disease: Tomita prognostic scoring system16
Tumor extent in relation to the neural elements: Epidural Spinal Cord Compression (ESCC)
classification17
Spinal stability: Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS)18
Classification-based treatment decision algorithm: Neurologic, oncologic, mechanical, and
systemic framework
Surgery on the Spine
General indications for spinal surgery
Spinal instability
Cord compression in patients with radioresistant tumor histology (eg, renal cell)
Oligometastatic disease in which a potential cure is tenable
Tumor separation surgery: new technique
Stabilizes the spine and decompresses neural elements via limited dissection
Allows for adjuvant high-dose radiation therapy to attain local tumor control
Management
Evolving Treatment Framework
Classification
The Harrington Classification for Spinal Metastasis

The Harrington Classification for Spinal Metastasis

The Harrington Classification for Spinal Metastasis15 is a comprehensive classification
system that was introduced in 1986 and is based on anatomic tumor characteristics. It
does not consider tumor biology or systemic patient factors.
The Harrington classification of spinal lesions involves five classes:
Class I: no considerable neurologic involvement
Class II: involvement of bone without collapse of instability
Class III: major neurologic involvement without any involvement of bone
Class IV: vertebral collapse with pain from mechanical causes but without any
neurologic compromise
Class V: vertebral collapse in combination with neurologic changes
Class I and class II lesions can be managed nonsurgically. Class III lesions can be
managed nonsurgically or surgically; evidence shows that if no bone is involved, these
lesions often will respond well to radiation therapy alone rather than surgical
decompression, depending on the histology and radiosensitivity of the lesion. Class IV
and V lesions will not improve with radiation therapy given bone instability. These lesions
require surgical decompression and fusion.15
Tomita Prognostic Scoring System

Tomita Prognostic Scoring System
In 2001, Tomita et al16 developed the Tomita prognostic scoring system, which
complemented and improved on the Harrington classification for spinal metastasis by
including systemic patient factors and prognostic estimates into the decision-making
framework.
The Tomita prognostic scoring system involves three factors:
Factor 1: primary tumor

9/3/26, 4:05 PM
AAOS | Evaluation and Management of Spinal Metastases

11/24

Factor 2: visceral metastases
Factor 3: bone metastases
In the Tomita prognostic scoring system, patient prognosis guides management. The
primary tumor category is stratified into slow growth (1 point), including breast, thyroid,
and prostate cancer; moderate growth (2 points), including kidney and uterine cancer;
and rapid growth (4 points), including lung, liver, stomach, and colon cancer. Visceral
metastases are divided into three categories: no visceral metastases (0 points), visceral
metastases that can be managed surgically (2 points), and visceral metastases that
cannot be managed surgically (4 points). Bone metastases are divided into two
categories: solitary or isolated spine metastasis (1 point) and multiple spinal or other
osseous metastases (2 points). The authors reported that the mean survival was 50
months for patients with 2 to 3 points, 24 months for patients with 4 to 5 points, 15
months for patients with 6 to 7 points, and 6 months for patients with 8 or more points.
They recommended en bloc spondylectomy for patients with 2 to 3 points, intralesional
or marginal excision for patients with 4 to 5 points, spinal cord decompression and
stabilization for patients with 6 to 7 points, and nonsurgical treatment for patients with 8
or more points. The authors acknowledged that surgical treatment must be made on a
case-by-case basis after extensive discussion with the patient.16
Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy

Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
Given the advent of stereotactic body radiation therapy, the treatment algorithm for
metastatic spinal tumors was revolutionized. This treatment modality allows for the
delivery of tumoricidal doses of radiation to the spinal column with excellent precision,
allowing the tumor to be targeted while sparing the surrounding structures (spinal cord
or cauda equina). This has obviated the need for total en bloc spondylectomy for tumor
control.

Indications for Surgical Management in the Era of Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
Spinal instability
High-grade cord compression in patients with a radio-insensitive tumor19 (Resource 3)
Solitary bone metastasis in select patients with curative intent

Pain presentation in the context of spinal metastasis can be described as mechanical
predominant, radiculopathy dominant, and myelopathy dominant, and considerable
treatment implications exist for each. Mechanical pain is best managed via stabilization,
whereas radiculopathy- and myelopathy-dominant pain are best managed via a
combination of surgical decompression and radiation therapy guided by the degree of
compression and tumor histology.
For patients with a SINS score lower than 6 who will be proceeding with radiation
therapy as the primary tumor treatment modality, adjuvant therapy, such as
radiofrequency ablation and kyphoplasty with polymethyl methacrylate augmentation,
may be used a to provide more immediate patient comfort and improve the tolerance of
radiation therapy.20
To decrease surgical dissection and wound-healing concerns with regard to unstable
spinal anatomy involved in metastatic disease, the concept of separation surgery (first
described at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center21) was developed. This involves a

limited posterolateral tumor resection followed by posterior segmental fixation and then
by postoperative single-fraction stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) at a tumoricidal dose (24
Gy), hypofractionated SRS at a high dose (24 to 30 Gy in three fractions), or
hypofractionated SRS at a low dose (20 to 30 Gy in three fractions). This serves as an
alternative to conventional total en bloc spondylectomy for durable tumor
control. Limited anterior body resection is performed using this treatment algorithm,
and cage reconstruction is indicated only if more than 50% of the vertebral body is
resected. A margin of 2 mm of separation from the dural elements is recommended for
the anticipated margin of radiation error that often occurs with stereotactic body
radiation therapy. For patients with a tumor intimately associated with the dura in whom
resection without dural breach is not possible, phosphorus 32 plaque can be used
intraoperatively for durable tumor control.22
Laufer et al23 reported that spinal instability should be managed surgically; however, In
patients with spinal cord compression because of radiosensitive tumor types, these can
be effectively managed via confocal external beam radiation therapy. In patients with
radio-insensitive tumors and cord compression, surgical decompression and fusion with
postoperative SRS is indicated. Long-term tumor control afforded by SRS obviates the
need for complete tumor resection independent of previous radiation therapy or the
pre-radiation/pre-decompression anatomic extent of tumor extension.

Neurologic factors: ESCC
Oncologic factors: Radiosensitivity of tumor
Mechanical stability: SINS score
Systemic: Subjective assessment of overall clinical presentation

Minimally Invasive Treatment Options

Minimally Invasive Treatment Options
In patients with a SINS score lower than 6 who have pain from tumor infiltration into
bone and a resultant compression fracture, kyphoplasty with radiofrequency ablation
may yield excellent pain relief and is used as an adjunct to radiation therapy. Improved
pain after kyphoplasty may allow for better tolerability of positioning for radiation
therapy.20
Postoperative Management

Postoperative Management
The major goal of postoperative management is early patient mobilization, discharge
home, and resumption of systemic therapy. Mobilization should begin on the first
postoperative day or as tolerated thereafter. Mechanical thromboprophylaxis is
preferred; however, chemical thromboprophylaxis also may be considered 48 hours
postoperatively in select patients. Postoperative radiation therapy may begin after the
incisions have adequately healed. The timing of postoperative resumption of systemic
therapy involves a collaborative discussion between the patient, the medical oncologist,
the radiation oncologist, and the surgeon, and it often is staggered to follow radiation
therapy. Diphosphonate or denosumab therapy is suggested to decrease the risk of
skeleton-related events in patients with no contraindications to therapy. Collaboration

with medical and radiation oncology colleagues is essential to provide excellent
comprehensive oncologic care.
Complications

Complications
The best method to avoid complications is to understand potential complications and
take steps to prevent them preoperatively, intraoperatively, and postoperatively.
Appropriate training and adherence to surgical principles is paramount. Potential
complications should be discussed with prospective patients and should be included in
consent documentation. Surgical treatment should be performed by a fellowship-trained
spine surgeon familiar with oncologic principles. Appropriate medical optimization
should be obtained preoperatively, neurophysiologic monitoring should be used
intraoperatively, care should be taken to delineate patient and tumor anatomy, and the
utmost attention should be paid to tissue handling.

Chronic pain
Misplaced hardware
Dural tearing

hardware

Chronic pain

Vascular injury

Urinary tract infection
Deep venous thrombosis
Pulmonary embolus
Pressure ulceration or nerve palsy secondary to patient positioning

therapy
Outcomes
The approach for patients with spinal metastatic disease is best summarized by using the
neurologic, oncologic, mechanical, and systemic framework.
Neurologic factors: ESCC
A clinical assessment of neurologic function
MRI-based scoring system of neurologic compression
Oncologic factors: radiosensitivity of the tumor
Patients with a radiosensitive tumor, such as myeloma, often can undergo radiation
therapy without surgical decompression with equivalent neurologic results.
More radio-insensitive pathologies require targeted radiation therapy and surgical
decompression.
Mechanical stability: SINS score
Mechanical instability is an indication for surgical stabilization.
In patients with tumors and mechanical stability of the spine, pain control may be
approached via less invasive methods, such as polymethyl methacrylate augmentation with
kyphoplasty
Systemic: subjective assessment of overall clinical presentation
The patient must always remain central to any discussion of metastatic disease.
The overall health state and wishes of the patient are the most important factors to be
considered in determining the course of treatment.
